title: Eutychus (Acts 20:7–12)
hookLine: a young man falls asleep during Paul's long sermon and falls from a window

lines: A YOUNG MAN IN A WINDOW.
cards: A long homily, a late lecture, a meeting that runs past its hour: the Bible has a story for that. And the long speaker isn't some dull preacher. It's the Apostle Paul.
The listener who nods off is a young man named Eutychus, sitting in an open window, three floors up. The room is crowded, the hour is late, and the lamps are burning.
What happens next is both funny and serious, and it shows how one early church spent the first day of the week.

teach.h: THE FIRST DAY OF THE WEEK.
teach.b: It's Troas, a port on the coast of what is now Turkey. Luke sets the scene carefully, in the Douay-Rheims: "on the first day of the week, when we were assembled to break bread." We: the narrator was in the room.
Sunday, the church gathered for the breaking of the bread.
Paul is leaving the next day, so he has a lot to say, and he keeps talking until midnight. The upper room is crowded, with many lamps burning: warm, close and smoky.

A young man named Eutychus is sitting in the window. And the text, with a straight face, says he sank into a deep sleep as Paul talked on and on, fell from the third story, and was taken up dead. Everyone rushes down.
Paul goes down too, throws himself on the young man, embraces him, and says: don't be troubled, his life is in him. Then the part that makes people laugh.

teach.h: AND PAUL WENT ON UNTIL DAYBREAK.
teach.b: Paul goes back upstairs, breaks the bread, eats, and keeps talking until daybreak. A man fell out the window, and even so, Paul went on.
Meanwhile they bring the young man home alive, and the text says they were not a little comforted. His name, Eutychus, means fortunate. Luke may be smiling.
But under the humor is an early picture of Christians gathering on the first day of the week to break bread, which Catholics read as the Eucharist, with a long sermon attached.

how: Catholics gather on Sunday, the first day of the week, for Mass, where the homily follows the Gospel and the Eucharist follows the homily; Sunday Mass is an obligation for Catholics.

practice: Think of a speaker who tests your patience, a preacher, a teacher, a relative with long stories, a boss in meetings, and notice the impatience in your body.
Picture them as someone who cares about what they're saying and maybe lacks the gift of brevity, and let a little of the irritation go; if you're the long talker sometimes, smile at that too.
If you pray, pray for that person by name.

wordCard.voice: Eutychus. The young man whose name means fortunate, who fell asleep in a window during Paul's sermon, and was brought home alive. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: Eutychus, a name meaning fortunate or lucky. a fitting name for a man who fell three stories.
